questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${e}^{2x}={({e}^{x})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u={e}^{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2x}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{({e}^{x})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡{e}^{x}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $9{x}^{2}=(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{1-9{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1-(3x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|3x|<1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/12}\frac{2}{1-9{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{1/12}\frac{1}{1-(3x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/12}\frac{1}{1-9{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/12}\frac{1}{1-(3x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/4}\frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}\frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/4} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{1}{4})-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{1}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{12}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+9}}\,\text{d}x=4{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{12}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+9}}\,\text{d}x & =4{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =12\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =12\operatorname{arsinh}⁡2-12\operatorname{arsinh}⁡0 \\  & =12\operatorname{arsinh}⁡2 \\  & =12\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\sqrt{{2}^{2}+1}) \\  & =12\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$
